CRED Crunch 70, 74 and 78 (Year in Review 2022, 2023, 2024) print no flood totals or by-type tables.

After the blocked adsr_2020.pdf request, every further WebFetch was refused as 'PROVENANCE_REQUIRED' (CredCrunch66.pdf for 2021, CredCrunch54.pdf for 2018, a re-read of the 2023 report), so those cross-checks were not made.

https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/number-of-deaths-from-natural-disasters-by-type (a secondary re-publication of EM-DAT yearly flood deaths, grade C at best) returned a fetch error; not pursued further because the task asks for CRED's own publications.

WebSearch: the shared search budget ran out after nine searches (used for the ADSR 2010, 2011, 2012, 2014, 2015 and CRED Crunch file locations), so the IFRC World Disasters Report annex tables (EM-DAT deaths by type and year, compiled by CRED, which would cover 2010 and 2012) and any EM-DAT HTML summary pages for 2022 to 2024 could not be searched for.
notes: Status partial: CRED-printed all-cause flood death counts were found for 9 of the 15 years (2011; 2013 to 2019; 2021), one of them (2019) already in the ledger and confirmed. Missing: 2010 (ADSR 2010 and CRED Crunch 23 print no flood total), 2012 (only the hydrological sub-group, 3,574, recorded as its own clearly scoped row), 2020 (the newsletter prints a 41% share and the 2000 to 2019 average 5,233; the full report was blocked), and 2022 to 2024 (the reports carry the counts only as bar labels in Figure 4, whose text layer could not be paired with the type labels). Two kinds of provenance: (a) printed sentences for 2011, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and the 2004 to 2013, 2005 to 2014, 2006 to 2015 and 2000 to 2019 averages; (b) bar labels read from the Figure 4 text layer for 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021 and the 2007 to 2016, 2008 to 2017, 2009 to 2018 and 2001 to 2020 averages. Every (b) value is kept only where the nine values in label order sum exactly to the report's own printed total (2017: 9,697; 2018: 11,804; 2021: 10,492; averages 68,274, 67,572, 45,212), or, for 2019, where the eight recovered values plus one missing value match 11,755 and the Flood value equals the printed 43.5% share; the 2001 to 2020 average row fails its sum check (64,399 against 61,212) and is flagged. A person with a PDF viewer should confirm each (b) bar label. Revisions recorded rather than chosen: 2015 is printed as 3,310 (CRED Crunch 41, February 2016) and 3,449 (ADSR 2015); 2011's 5,202 comes from a February 2012 newsletter whose total (29,780) the July 2012 ADSR raised to 30,773 without reprinting a flood count; 2013's 9,819 is called both 'floods' and 'hydrological disasters' in the same report. CRED's rolling averages fall through the decade (6,293; 5,933; 5,709; 5,553; 5,039; 4,913) and then sit near 5,200 on twenty-year windows (5,233; 5,185). The one grade-D row applies who-flood-share to the mean of the nine sourced years (3,525); it is explicitly not the 15-year mean the task asked for, and flood-drowning-band is not retired. Candidate values a person should check, NOT recorded as findings: in the 2022 report's Figure 4 text layer the value 7,574 sits where a flood bar label would be expected, and in the 2023 report's the value 7,763 (the 2023 report counts the Libya Storm Daniel floods, 12,352 deaths, in its text as a storm-caused flood event, so its type assignment matters); neither could be tied to a label or total. The 2020 report URL is emdat.be/sites/default/files/adsr_2020.pdf. Grade A rows whose file was read in a university or ALNAP mirror (2012, 2013, 2015) carry the cred.be URL from CRED's own publication index and say so in their notes. No names, contact details or precise positions were recorded; author names seen in report front matter were deliberately left out. Nothing was summed or averaged outside the grade-D row; any two-row sum coincidence the checker flags (e.g. 4,731 + 379 = 5,110 against an unrelated US pool row) is accidental, since no row here was built from other rows.
